column4: Everyone in this square says they're fine.
In a second, you'll see the storms they're hiding.
This morning, you woke up and saw weather. Not outside. Over people's heads.
Sun means they're doing fine. Clouds, rain, storms mean they're not. And their faces? Their faces never change.
Three rules. One: you can see everyone's inner weather. Two: they can't. Three: the only weather you can't see is your own.
He was not doing great.
Once you see it, you see it everywhere.
Bea, the baker, smiling behind her counter. A small cloud. Some days, that inner critic still talks.
Finn, the island's joker, cracking jokes on his boat. Drizzle.
Kai, the builder. Calm, steady, always fine. A storm.
And you'd thought you were the only one having a rough week.
When researchers asked students to guess how many classmates had recently been through something hard, they guessed too low. And the lower the guess, the lonelier they tended to feel.
So why don't we see it?
Because we hide the rain and show the sunshine. In the same research, students kept about forty percent of their bad moments to themselves. Their good moments? Only thirteen percent.
Most feeds are sunny, even when the sky isn't.
Then you see Ana.
Ana, who said hello to a lonely stranger every day for a month. Ana, who shows up for everyone.
Ana has the biggest storm on the island.
So you ask how she's doing.
And then you ask again. No, really. How are you?
You tell her to ask. Just ask.
In one experiment, people guessed they'd have to ask about twenty strangers to get five to do a small favor. They needed about ten.
We're sure we'll be a burden. But people say yes far more often than we expect.
And then Ana does something nobody's done all week.
For the first time, you catch your reflection in the window. Your own weather.
A cloud. Not the biggest. Not the smallest. Just weather, like everyone's.
You were never the only one.
You'll never see anyone's weather. But you can ask how someone's doing, and if they say fine, ask one more time. And if you're the one under the storm, let someone help. They'll probably say yes.
Everyone's carrying some weather. You don't have to carry yours alone.
